# Frame Job [![Frame Job in 90 seconds: watch on YouTube](https://img.youtube.com/vi/An7KjPoofzI/maxresdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_xkkMhgNRQU) A native macOS video editor. Open a movie, arrange it on layered tracks over a fixed canvas, then trim, cut, grade, caption, animate and export it. Every edit you make in the window can also be made by an AI agent over MCP, or by the built-in Assistant, and each one is an ordinary undo step. Apple Silicon, macOS 26 or later. There is no account to make: every AI feature runs on your own API key (Anthropic for the Assistant, AssemblyAI for cloud transcription), and everything else works without one. ## Open a movie and start cutting **File ▸ Open…** (⌘O) on a `.mov` or `.mp4` — or a drop on the Dock icon, or **Open Video…** in the Welcome window — creates an *untitled* project sized and rated to that file, with the file as the first clip on Track 1, ready to cut. A portrait phone clip opens portrait, and a 29.97 fps file stays 29.97. **Save** then writes a `.framejob` package, offered next to the source. ## Features **Projects and media.** Movies, sound and pictures from everything macOS plays, plus WebM and MKV copied in without re-encoding; missing files relinked; Consolidate Media copies footage into the package. → [Projects and media](docs/guide/projects-and-media.md) **Timeline.** One kind of track that holds any clip; a frame-accurate ruler, filmstrips and waveforms, zoom about the cursor, snapping, markers, an in/out range, track mute, solo and lock, clip names and colour labels. → [The timeline and playback](docs/guide/timeline.md) **Editing.** Move, nudge, trim, slip, roll, split, lift, ripple delete, close gap, insert time, insert and overwrite, copy and paste, Paste Attributes, and nests that group clips into one.

content.text:
I've added the table to `README.md`, right under the YouTube link:

| Language | Code | Test |
|---|--:|--:|
| Swift | 80,760 | 52,303 |
| Rust | 22,400 | 54,131 |
| Metal | 1,682 | — |
| JavaScript | 755 | 2,669 |
| TypeScript | 754 | 238 |
| Python | 739 | 131,328 |
| C header | 144 | 6 |
| Shell | 46 | 109 |
| **Total** | **107,280** | **240,784** |

How I counted:
- **What a line is:** lines that aren't blank or comments, counted by `cloc` over the files git tracks. The vendored copy of tiny-skia in `graphic/vendor` and the prototypes in `designs/` are left out. Markdown, JSON and TOML files aren't counted either.
- **Code:** `app/Sources`, the source of the three Rust crates, the C headers, the Metal shaders, the graphics engine's JavaScript standard library, the assistant helper's non-test TypeScript, and the build scripts in `tools/codecs` and `tools/licenses`.
- **Test:** the three Rust crates' `tests/` folders, the helper's `*.test.ts` files, the licence generator's self-test, and all of `tools/proof/`. That folder includes the design spikes, which account for much of the Swift test count and some of the Rust. If you'd rather count only real tests, say so and I'll move the spikes out of the Test column.

Under the table there's a short note saying how the counts were made. The README already had an uncommitted change to the video link, and I left it as it was. Nothing is committed.

content.text:
I committed the README as `a3e97f9` and pushed `main`. The commit includes both changes: the new video link and the line-count table. Nothing else was staged.

The push also sent `b71e20b` (Graphic browser phase 1), which was already committed on `main` but hadn't been pushed yet. Nothing went to the `publish` branch, so no release build was started.

The table is a one-off count: nothing in the build updates it, so the numbers will drift as the code changes.
